stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
stimulus: An ecologist lays out two straight survey trails, $\ell$ and $m$, across a meadow, and a straight fence line $t$ crosses both of them. Line $t$ intersects line $\ell$ at point $P$ and line $m$ at point $Q$. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on line $\ell$ on opposite sides of $P$. Points $C$ and $D$ lie on line $m$ on opposite sides of $Q$. Points $A$ and $C$ are on the same side of line $t$. Point $E$ lies on line $t$ so that $P$ is between $E$ and $Q$. The measure of $\angle EPA$ is $72^\circ$.
explanation: Ray $PE$ and ray $QP$ point the same way along $t$, and $A$ and $C$ are on the same side of $t$. That makes $\angle EPA$ and $\angle PQC$ corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel, so $m\angle PQC = 72^\circ$ is sufficient.

A.why: $\angle QPB$ and $\angle EPA$ are vertical angles, so they are equal whenever two lines cross. This choice tells you nothing about line $m$, so it can't prove the lines are parallel.

B.why: $\angle APQ$ and $\angle EPA$ form a linear pair, so they always add up to $180^\circ$. You picked a fact that is true at point $P$ no matter where line $m$ is.

D.why: $\angle APQ$ ($108^\circ$) and $\angle PQC$ are same-side interior angles, and you treated them as if they had to be equal. They need to add up to $180^\circ$, so the lines are parallel only when $\angle PQC$ is $72^\circ$. If it is $108^\circ$, the lines are not parallel.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $JKL$ is similar to triangle $RST$?
stimulus: A marine biologist marks two triangular survey plots on a coral reef. In triangle $JKL$, $JK = 6$ meters and $KL = 9$ meters. In triangle $RST$, $RS = 4$ meters and $ST = 6$ meters.
explanation: $\frac{JK}{RS} = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{KL}{ST} = \frac{9}{6} = \frac{3}{2}$, so two pairs of sides are in proportion. Angle $K$ lies between $JK$ and $KL$, and angle $S$ lies between $RS$ and $ST$. If those included angles are equal, the triangles are similar by SAS similarity.

B.why: Angle $L$ is not between the two proportional sides, so this is side-side-angle. SSA doesn't fix the shape of a triangle, so it can't prove similarity.

C.why: You matched the included angle of $JKL$ with the wrong angle of $RST$. Angle $T$ is not between $RS$ and $ST$, so the sides and the angle don't line up as SAS similarity requires.

D.why: This does give you a third pair of sides, but $\frac{12}{9} = \frac{4}{3}$, which is not the $\frac{3}{2}$ ratio of the other pairs. SSS similarity needs all three ratios to match, and here they don't.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $XYZ$?
stimulus: An archaeologist records two triangular sections of a mosaic floor as triangles $PQR$ and $XYZ$. Angle $Q$ and angle $Y$ are right angles, and $PQ = XY$.
choices: $m\angle P + m\angle R = m\angle X + m\angle Z$
explanation: Both triangles are right triangles, and leg $PQ$ equals leg $XY$. $PR$ and $XZ$ are the hypotenuses, since each is opposite a right angle. If the hypotenuses are equal too, the triangles are congruent by Hypotenuse-Leg (HL).

A.why: $XZ$ is the hypotenuse of triangle $XYZ$, but $QR$ is a leg of triangle $PQR$. You set a leg equal to a hypotenuse, which doesn't match corresponding parts, so no congruence criterion is completed.

C.why: This only tells you about triangle $PQR$. With no matching fact about triangle $XYZ$, you have nothing to compare, so you can't prove congruence.

D.why: In any right triangle the two acute angles add up to $90^\circ$, so this equation is always true. It only restates the right angles you already had and adds no new fact to compare.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
stimulus: A printmaker carves two straight grooves, lines $\ell$ and $m$, into a linoleum block, then makes a straight diagonal cut, line $t$, that crosses both grooves. Angle 1 is formed where $t$ meets $\ell$, and angle 2 is formed where $t$ meets $m$. Angles 1 and 2 are same-side interior angles. The measure of angle 1 is $64^\circ$.
choices: The angle vertical to angle 1 measures $64^\circ$.
The angle forming a linear pair with angle 1 measures $116^\circ$.
The angle forming a linear pair with angle 2 measures $64^\circ$.
Angle 2, the given interior angle, measures $64^\circ$.
explanation: If the angle forming a linear pair with angle 2 measures $64^\circ$, then angle 2 measures $180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$. Angles 1 and 2 are same-side interior angles, and $64^\circ + 116^\circ = 180^\circ$. Same-side interior angles that are supplementary prove the lines are parallel.

A.why: Vertical angles are always equal, so this is true wherever line $t$ crosses line $\ell$. It says nothing about line $m$ and can't prove the lines are parallel.

B.why: An angle forming a linear pair with angle 1 always measures $180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$. You picked a fact that is automatically true at line $\ell$ and tells you nothing about line $m$.

D.why: You treated same-side interior angles as if they had to be equal. They need to add up to $180^\circ$. If angle 2 is $64^\circ$, the sum is $128^\circ$, so the lines are not parallel.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$?
stimulus: An immunologist sketches two triangular regions of a cell-staining slide as triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$. In these triangles, $m\angle A = m\angle D = 40^\circ$ and $m\angle B = m\angle E = 75^\circ$.
explanation: Two pairs of angles are already equal: $\angle A$ with $\angle D$ and $\angle B$ with $\angle E$. Side $BC$ is opposite $\angle A$, and side $EF$ is opposite $\angle D$, so they are corresponding sides. Adding $BC = EF$ gives Angle-Angle-Side, which proves the triangles are congruent.

A.why: You can already get the third angles from the $180^\circ$ sum, so this is a step on the way rather than new information. Three pairs of equal angles prove the triangles are similar, but they can still be different sizes. Angles alone (AAA) never prove congruence.

B.why: $AB$ is opposite $\angle C$, but $EF$ is opposite $\angle D$, so these sides don't correspond. Making them equal would only scale one triangle relative to the other. It doesn't force the triangles to be the same size.

D.why: The triangles are already similar by AA, so corresponding sides are automatically in proportion. This ratio is true for any scale factor, so it can't show that the triangles are the same size.

stimulus: A city planner sketches two triangular pocket parks, triangle $PQR$ and triangle $STU$, on a site map. In the sketch, the measure of angle $P$ is equal to the measure of angle $S$.
explanation: You already have one pair of equal angles: $\angle P$ and $\angle S$. Angle-angle (AA) similarity needs a second pair. If $m\angle Q = m\angle T$, two angles of triangle $PQR$ match two angles of triangle $STU$. The third angles must then match as well, because each triangle's angles sum to $180^\circ$. So triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $STU$.

A.why: You accepted proportional sides without checking which angle lies between them. Sides $PQ$ and $QR$ meet at angle $Q$, not at angle $P$, so the equal angle isn't the included one. C.why: This is only part of the way to SAS similarity. One side ratio, together with one pair of equal angles, doesn't fix the shape of either triangle. You would need a second pair of sides in the same ratio, both meeting at the equal angles, or a second pair of equal angles.

D.why: This gives the size of the angle you had already matched instead of a new pair of corresponding parts. Knowing that angles $P$ and $S$ both measure $40^\circ$ tells you nothing about angles $Q$, $R$, $T$, or $U$, so you still have only one pair of equal angles.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $p$ is parallel to line $q$?
stimulus: A paleobotanist traces two fossilized stems as lines $p$ and $q$, with line $p$ above line $q$. A straight crack, line $t$, crosses both. Where $t$ meets $p$, the angles are labeled clockwise from top left as $\angle 1$, $\angle 2$, $\angle 3$, and $\angle 4$. Where $t$ meets $q$, they are labeled the same way as $\angle 5$, $\angle 6$, $\angle 7$, and $\angle 8$.
explanation: Both $\angle 3$ and $\angle 7$ are in the bottom-right position at their intersection, so they are corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel. That makes this condition enough on its own to prove that $p \parallel q$.

A.why: You chose a pair of vertical angles. Vertical angles are equal whenever two lines cross, whether or not $p$ and $q$ are parallel, so this condition proves nothing about line $q$.

B.why: You chose a linear pair. Angles $5$ and $8$ sit next to each other along line $t$, so they always add to $180^\circ$. Because the condition is always true, it can't tell you whether the lines are parallel.

D.why: Angles $4$ and $5$ are same-side interior angles. To prove the lines are parallel, those angles have to add to $180^\circ$. Being equal isn't the right test. Saying they are equal proves parallel lines only in the special case where both are $90^\circ$.
